newsitem.title: CUBA: Cuban parliament approves law against Helms-Burton.
newsitem.headline: Cuban parliament approves law against Helms-Burton.

text.p: Cuba's National Assembly has approved legislation aimed at countering the U.S. Helms-Burton law that toughened Washington's longstanding economic embargo against Havana.

The Law of Reaffimration of Cuban Dignity and Sovereignty was approved late on Tuesday by the parliament, which was holding a two-day session on Tuesday and Wednesday. The new Cuban law declares Helms-Burton inapplicable and without value.
President Fidel Castro, attending the session, described the law as a patriotic move that would also protect and give confidence for foreign investors in Cuba.

U.S. President Bill Clinton dropped earlier reservations and approved the Republican-sponsored Helms-Burton law in March following the downing the previous month by Cuban fighters of two small private U.S. planes flying near Cuba.

Helms-Burton calls for radical political change in Cuba and includes controversial provisions to allow U.S. citizens to file law suits against foreign firms doing business on property expropriated from U.S. interests following Castro's 1959 revolution.
These provisions have been widely criticised by countries that do business with the communist-ruled island, such as Mexico, Canada and European Union members.

The new Cuban law declares invalid any claim made under Helms-Burton. It says that those persons in the United States seeking to make claims under Helms-Burton would be exempt from any future possible U.S.-Cuba settlement on the property issue.

The document re-states the Cuban government's willingness to negotiate compensation for U.S. citizens whose holdings in Cuba were nationalised after the revolution. Cuba argues that such compensation discussions should form part of wider negotiation and should take place on the basis of mutual respect, not pressure from the United States.

The new law also authorises the Cuban government to take measures to protect existing and future foreign investors on the island. One proposal to protect foreign investors is to allow the transfer of investment interests into trust funds.
The Cuban law also declares the right of Cubans to claim compensation for damages caused by U.S. policies and actions, including the 34-year-old embargo.
In addition to approving the "antidote" to Helms-Burton, the Cuban parliament also on Tuesday approved the country's economic plan for 1997 and the state budget.

Presenting the plan, Economy Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez said the country had achieved higher than expected economic growth in 1996. Cuba would now aim for a slower rate of recovery as it seeks a sustainable level of growth and tries to rein in its trade deficit.

Rodriguez said Gross Domestic Product (GDP) growth in 1996 would be 7.8 percent, better than a forecast five percent and above last year's 2.5 percent growth, despite what he called exceptionally difficult conditions.

The minister said the 1997 economic plan foresaw GDP growth of four to five percent. The main goal of the plan would be to achieve an improved balance of payments as the basis for sustainable development, he said, without giving figures.
Cuba's largely state-controlled economy is emerging from sharp contraction of more than 35 percent between 1989 and 1993, triggered by the collapse of the former Soviet Union.
